Then, sir, dealing with the amendment which I should like to move at this stage, there are one or two observations I should like to make. First, this is an exceptional motion in that the regular 48 hours' notice has not been given. Because of that fact it seems to me there should be greater scope given to the inquiry than that contained in the motion made by the minister. If there is reason to investigate the toll collection operations at Jacques Cartier bridge, it seems to me there is also reason to consider the toll collection operations at nearby Victoria bridge. After all, if there are reasons which exist in the one case those reasons exist in the other as well. If we do not consider the other case, then we will only be dealing with half the problem; and if there is anything to be investigated we on this side of the house feel that the whole problem should be considered at this time.
That is why I believe the scope of the investigation should be broad enough to contain a reference which would cover the operations of the other bridge. I know that when the matter is considered in the committee there are bound to be some hon. members who will rise and want to know what the position is with respect to the other bridge. They will want to know the methods by which tolls are collected on the other bridge. The chairman of the committee will be bound to say that the powers of reference of the committee do not include Victoria bridge and have reference only to Jacques Cartier bridge. Therefore it seems to me that the committee should be empowered to go further and consider the whole problem of the toll collection operations of these two bridges.
I said earlier that this is not the kind of investigation that we think the house should make, because such an investigation is bound to be an anaemic one. It seems to me that a judicial inquiry into a matter of

this kind should have been entered upon. I am precluded by the rules from moving an amendment to that effect, but I am going to move an amendment which will cover not only the toll collection operations on the Jacques Cartier bridge but that with respect to the Victoria bridge where the operations, as the house knows, are also carried on by Canadian National Railways, an emanation of the crown which reports to the house through the Minister of Transport. Therefore it would strike me that there should be no objection to the amendment.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill):
That the period be struck out and that a semicolon be substituted therefor, with the following added thereto:
"and at the Victoria bridge, Montreal, Quebec."

Citation 291 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, reads as follows:
When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given-
I interpolate that I think the principle would be the same because this motion is treated as though notice had been given, the house having given unanimous consent that it be proceeded with. I continue with the citation:
-for the appointment of a select committee, a member cannot move in amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice.
Then there are some examples, and at the foot of the page the following:
The Speaker ruled both amendments out of order on the ground that they raised new questions not contemplated in the notice of motion and proposed to extend the committee's powers far beyond those set down in the notice, and also that the necessity of giving notice will be nullified if such notice is not used as a guidance for the decision of the house.

At this point I should like to commend the Minister of Agriculture for what he has done in this regard. When the brucellosis control program was introduced in the province of

Ontario in 1958 the compensation for animals slaughtered under the regulations was quite inadequate and out of date. In July of 1958 the house passed legislation recommended by the minister which increased the compensation paid for animals slaughtered. At the same time it made the compensation retroactive to April 1, 1958. This was a splendid move by the minister, I might say, and was greatly appreciated by all concerned.

The brucellosis control program was introduced in the province of Ontario in 1958, as I have already mentioned, and the control was designed to be province-wide. The first two counties where the program was started were the counties of Oxford and Prince Edward.
During the month of March, 1958 veterinarians of the federal Department of Agriculture went around examining animals in these two counties, and a number of animals in both counties were found to be reactors and were ordered to be slaughtered. A number of farmers in both counties, anxious to cooperate with the government's program in this respect, complied immediately with the request of the veterinarians and sent the animals to be slaughtered. As a result, 48 farmers in the county of Oxford and 16 in the county of Prince Edward sent their animals to be slaughtered prior to March 31 of that year. As a result those farmers did not receive the increased rate of compensation that the rest of the farmers in their own counties received, and indeed that the rest of the farmers in the province of Ontario received.
I realize that the minister has considerable difficulty in this regard, because he was good enough to recommend legislation to make these payments retroactive and which, included the counties which entered this program at an early stage. I have already thanked the minister for that because it was a good piece of legislation. I realize also that by making this legislation for increased payments retroactive to April the minister took it back to the beginning of the fiscal year. I realize that is something that probably had to be done. However, it seems to me rather unfair, on the face of it, that a few farmers in these two counties, chiefly because they chose to cooperate with the program with great alacrity, should be penalized.
That is in effect what has happened. Those farmers whose animals were condemned in March, 1958 and who, for one reason or another, did not send the animals in to be
Supply-Agriculture
slaughtered until April, received the compensation. Those who sent their animals in right away did not get the increased compensation. It does seem to me rather unfair to these people in these two counties. I think you have to look at this question as a facet of the larger picture. The plan in Ontario was to make the whole province free of brucellosis. The fact that each county decided to carry out this program at a different time I think is an inmportant aspect of the whole picture. A few farmers, for the reasons I have stated, missed out on the increased compensation.
I believe this fact could be considered, and I hope the minister will give further consideration to it. I believe the estimated cost is approximately $3,800 in the county of Oxford and approximately $1,600 in the county of Prince Edward. I am fully aware of the argument the minister has advanced, and I can see the logic of it. It is that since the brucellosis control program had been under way in isolated areas in other parts of the country, some in Prince Edward Island and some out west, in 1956 and 1957, if these payments were made retroactive to a greater degree those areas would have to be taken into consideration as well.
I do not believe I can agree with that, in view of the fact that these were isolated instances and there was not a province-wide program. In the instances to which I refer in Ontario they were part of a program for the entire province. It has been suggested to me that perhaps other hon. members representing other parts of the country might object if these payments were made to these few farmers in Prince Edward and Oxford counties. I feel that any fair-minded person from any other part of the country would not object to these payments being made, in view of the circumstances, and would not insist that the government make this compensation retroactive to 1956. In view of the fact all parts of the country are represented in this house-I do not want to sound like the minister at a wedding-I would say that if any of them have any objections to these payments they should speak now, otherwise their silence could be taken as assent.
I realize it would be awkward for the minister to recommend further legislation in connection with this matter, but I do not believe that would be necessary. Perhaps the minister can correct me on that. In view of the fact that this increased compensation has been authorized by statute I believe the payments could be made by means of a supplementary estimate. I just put this to the minister in the hope that he will give it further consideration.

The difficulties in connection with this matter, Mr. Chairman, are the same difficulties which exist when any cut-off date is put into legislation for any purpose. There are always some people who are just beyond the cut-off date, in some cases by a day, in some cases by a week, and in some cases by a month. The people who have failed to secure the extra compensation as a result of having their cattle slaughtered a few days before the increased rate of compensation became effective naturally feel they should be entitled to as much as the people whose cattle were slaughtered after that date. Of course the same thing applies in any sort of program under which public funds are being paid out and in which a cut-off date exists.
These particular cattle in Oxford county cannot be considered by themselves. They in fact would not be the only ones affected by setting back the date. There would be cattle in several provinces in Canada that would be affected by this action. The date after which the increased amount of compensation for animals slaughtered was to be effective was contained in legislation put through this house in June or July. We set the date back at that time to the beginning of the financial year. I do not believe we can go any farther than that. It would be completely unfair to make a special payment to the farmers in Oxford county, whom the hon. member is representing, and not make it to farmers in other provinces across Canada who had cattle slaughtered in that same period.
If we set the date back one week or two weeks, whatever the case might be, there would immediately be a demand, and a justified demand, that we should set it back another two weeks or two months. I believe once you have set a date in a matter of this kind it is not good policy, and is not fair to everybody concerned across the country, to set it back another week at a subsequent time in order to take in a few persons who feel that they were just cut out by the date set at that time.
I understood the hon. member for Oxford to say that this was confined to the county of Oxford, or to areas immediately adjacent to that county.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Prince Edward county as well.
The minister says it applies in many places and counties. I wonder what the facts are, those stated by the Minister of Agriculture or by the hon. member for Oxford.

The hon. member for Oxford was talking about the brucellosis eradication program in the province of Ontario, but this

brucellosis eradication program has been going on since April of 1957. He mentioned that one of the first places to go into the complete eradication program was Prince Edward Island. There would, as a result, be a considerable number of people who had cattle slaughtered as part of the brucellosis testing program prior to this date. In addition, animals slaughtered for any purpose would have to be considered. It would not be fair to say those people who had cattle slaughtered as part of the brucellosis program will be paid, but their neighbours who had cattle slaughtered as part of the tuberculosis program will not be paid. You would have to make it applicable to animals that were slaughtered for any purpose under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
I should like to make a brief statement in connection with the reasons for the increased amount of money needed under this vote at this particular time. The expenditures for the brucellosis eradication program have increased very materially during the past several months. As I stated a month ago, the program was started in April of 1957, but during the past eight or nine months particularly the demand on the part of various counties and municipalities for the program to be put into effect has increased greatly as the realization grew throughout the country of the necessity for and the value of this eradication program. As a result we have carried on a great deal more testing than the experience up to the past several months would indicate would have been the case. As a result of the great increase in the amount of testing there is the necessity for this increased vote.
Of course the faster this is done, the better for the cattle industry and for the human population of this country, and actually the cheaper in the long run the whole program will be to accomplish. Also part of the increase is due to the fact that we were obliged to put into effect a new scrapie control program in August, I believe it was, of this year-it was either August or September, but I believe it was in August-in view of the fact that several of the American states had placed embargoes on Canadian sheep and lamb going into those areas on the basis that our scrapie program in Canada was not as stringent as that in the United States. In order to ensure that those markets were reopened and would remain open to our sheep and lamb people, we were obliged to increase the stringency of our scrapie regulation, a matter which involved considerably increased numbers of sheep and lambs being slaughtered.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this particular item. As the committee may know, we have had in Timiska-ming a serious outbreak of rabies which has involved some rethinking, I believe, in connection with our rabies control program. I do not know how many cases there were last year in the southern ridings, particularly in Grey, Bruce and Wellington, but I understand that serious outbreaks have taken place in that area. In my opinion they do not get enough publicity and are not discussed widely enough so that the general public is given enough information to enable them to protect themselves.
As you probably know, Mr. Chairman, this fall a child in the Port Credit area died from being bitten or scratched by a skunk; and because the parents did not know that this skunk could be rabid or was rabid, they did not take the precaution of seeing that the child had the inoculations which are necessary in such a case and of course the child died.
Many people do not realize that if you are bitten by a rabid animal of any kind, or if you come in contact with a cow that has been bitten and is rabid, you are in danger. If you come in contact with the saliva of that cow and it enters into a cut or an abrasion, unless you are given needles you will die, so I am told, one of the most horrible deaths possible. I am told that the disease affects your brain and your muscular system, and that death from this cause is probably as painful as any of which we know.
I spoke to a gentleman in my area who had a cow die. He informed me that just shortly before she died

and one of the problems is that we have to let them die in order to be sure they have rabies-she tore the stanchion out of the cement floor, broke the chain on that stanchion, took one of her horns and put a half-inch gouge in the cement floor, and finally lifted up four or five inches of concrete when she came to a place where there was a crack in the floor. After having seen what happened and having been exposed himself he said there was no question on his part, or on the part of the members of his family who had been in contact with this animal, with respect to going to the doctor and getting the 14 needles in the stomach muscles that are necessary to prevent any chance of them getting rabies themselves.
I think this matter must be discussed. I believe it should be given more public attention because of the danger from the disease. In this recent outbreak in Timisk-aming I found that many farmers were willing 79951-0-50
Supply-Agriculture
to cover up the fact that one of their animals had been bitten and exposed to the disease for the simple reason that they did not understand what the Department of Agriculture is doing in this field; they did not understand the length of quarantine that would take place.
Then there is the question of cost. Everybody who was exposed to the disease had to take these needles and considerable cost resulted. While the governments, provincial and federal, provide free serum for the inoculations, I am told by the doctors in my area that the cost of each needle is $2. It is necessary to take at least 14 needles and in some cases up to 21. If there are four or five members of the family the expense involved amounts to well over $200. Having regard to the fact that in some of the communities in my area the people are 150 miles away from the doctor, if they must be brought out to the doctor every day this situation could be a calamity for many who might be affected.
It would appear that in Timiskaming this outbreak was not a reinfection caused by the moving north, as was asserted, of a number of people from the southern area. It appears that there was very little of the disease in the area when the outbreak took place in Timiskaming; there was no case known, according to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I asked the hon. member for Nipissing. He did not know of any case in Nipissing. I discussed the matter with a number of veterinarians, and learned that there have been very few cases since 1955 in the area between the counties of Bruce, Grey and others and Timiskaming. It would therefore appear that a great deal more work has to be done in our particular area on this subject by the department so this disease may be controlled in other ways than those by which we have been controlling it.
To anybody who came to the conclusion that it was not spread from one area to another it would be obvious that it must be maintained in any area by a carrier agent. It has been suggested in countries like Germany that this carrier agent can be an animal or even a bird, and that while these agents do not themselves develop the disease and may not even be susceptible to it, they may act as a carrier and infect other animals.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to discuss this matter if there is another opportunity to do so. I would just like to say on the general subject that rabies is a contagious disease and therefore I did not interrupt the hon. member until he got on to the special item which went into the estimates last year to cover compensation for rabies.
The department is, of course, well aware of the seriousness of rabies and has devoted a great deal of attention to the problem of controlling the disease and preventing its spread. In the hon. member's constituency we are starting a rabies inoculation or vaccination clinic for dogs and cats in Timis-kaming on February 8. The chief means of control of this disease is by preventing it from spreading; as hon. members may know, it is spread almost entirely by the biting animals. As regards domestic animals, most of the attention centres on dogs and cats, and this program of vaccination is carried on in order to prevent the spreading of the disease.
As far as the outbreak in Timiskaming is concerned, the total number of cases from 79951-0-50J

April 1, 1959 until February 5-today- amounted to 12 cattle and eight sheep. That is the total number of cases of rabies in domestic animals in that area in a period not far short of a year. In addition there were 34 foxes killed; 34 which were found to have rabies. This disease is established among the wildlife of our country over which, of course, the department has really no means of control. It is endemic in our wildlife, and from time to time there seems to be an upsurge for reasons not generally known. Then foxes, particularly, begin to bite domestic animals and in this way the disease spreads. The domestic animals can be treated but, as I say, we have really no means of controlling the wildlife.

On this item, may I ask the minister what precautions are taken against the spread of brucellosis through the movement of cattle and whether these precautions interfere seriously with the normal cattle trade? Last fall Alberta tried to establish a brucellosis free area. There was great misunderstanding about it which seems to lead to confusion.

As part of the control of
brucellosis and in order to protect the work which has been done in areas which have been inspected and declared to be free of brucellosis we have to take precautions to see that cattle can only move into a brucellosis control area from another area of equal health status if they have, in accordance with the regulations, passed a negative brucellosis blood test. Calves under eight months of age, steers, spayed heifers and official vaccinated cattle up to 36 months of age are not required to be blood tested.
Where class A and B fairs request the department provides supervision of all cattle entries, blood testing them when necessary to assure brucellosis freedom. The majority of class A and B fairs operate under this scheme. A brucellosis certification and blood testing service where necessary is also provided to recognized breed sales.
With respect to interference with normal trade, it is of course impossible to control disease on any basis without some trade restrictions. However, the regulations are enforced to cause a minimum of inconvenience. As an example, auction markets and stockyards within brucellosis control areas have been exempted from the regulations where the volume justifies it. This means that such market places are open to all cattle and only those cattle bought by owners living within control areas require to be certified in accordance with the brucellosis control regulations. In addition, in order to avoid the holding of

cattle pending blood test results, purchasers are allowed to move cattle to destination and have them dealt with at home.

Plant Products Division-
612. Freight assistance on western feed grains- further amount required, $3,500,000.

I should like to make a brief statement in connection with item 612. Expenditures for this purpose-freight assistance to move western feed grains to eastern Canada and British Columbia-amounted in 1958-59 to $20 million. The same amount was provided in the main estimates for 1959-60. This, of course, is really what one might call a statutory item. Under provisions already made we subsidize this transportation of feed grain and the amount we have to pay depends, naturally, on the amount moved. An additional $1 million was provided in the first supplementary estimates for this fiscal year. That was to take care of what was estimated to be the extra amount needed because of the increase in freight rates which took place. In addition, purchases of western feed grain by eastern poultry producers have been much heavier than they were a year ago, and an additional $3J million will be required.
In other words, this extra requirement is due to the fact that a considerably increased amount of grain will have been moved by the end of the fiscal year.
Is there any change in the formula of payment? The minister is asking us now for $3,500,000 extra. Is there any change in the bassic formula?

There was a change made as a result of the increase in the freight rates. I explained that in the house last year-early last summer-pointing out that when that change took place it threw out of balance the assistance provided in different parts of the country. The rates were therefore adjusted so that the cost to farmers of one hundred pounds of feed would be more or less the same in all areas rather than increased in some places and decreased in others because of the change in freight rates.

Does the $20 million item which the house provided to reduce freight rates following the last increase have any effect on the moneys provided for assistance with regard to grain being shipped to eastern Canada and British Columbia under this item? In other words, does the $20 million provided for a general revision of freight rates have any effect on this subsidy, or are the two things entirely separate?

It has an effect because if that $20 million subsidy had not been made

and the freight rate had not been reduced the amount required under this subsidy would be greater than it is.
When the freight rates did go up we put an item in the estimates for an extra million dollars beyond the $20 million expended last year. The only way in which we can really estimate this is on the basis of the experience in the past year, and as $20 million had been used last year we put $20 million in this year's estimate. Then when the freight rates were increased we put in a supplementary estimate for an extra million. Now we find, however, that the amount of grain which has been shipped has been much greater than last year and we therefore require this extra sum of $3,500,000.
That makes a total of $24,500,000?
Yes.

We in the C.C.F. party have always supported this item and we shall do so once again. We have opposed any move made in the past to reduce the basis for this payment. In other words, we have been opposed to successive increases in freight rates removing part of the advantage that has accrued from this item of expenditure.
This sum totalling $24,500,000 in the present fiscal year is paid for the movement of feed grains that are produced on the prairies to markets, feeders and farmers in central Canada, the maritimes and British Columbia. This is an important part of agricultural policy today. I think it is an essential one in the interests of agricultural producers outside the prairie provinces.
I want to make it clear that this is a substantial item which no doubt will receive the unanimous support of all hon. members. But this is an item that is not being paid to the prairie grain producers. The main advantage certainly does not accrue to them. This is an agricultural or freight subsidy, if you like, which is of substantial advantage to farmers outside the prairie provinces.
Coming as I do from Saskatchewan it is my pleasure to support this item as one that is a national advantage, the bulk of the advantage accruing to producers, feeders and farmers outside the prairie provinces.
In my opinion the government should consider the whole question of freight on agricultural products. This item is of advantage to producers outside the prairies and is paid by the national treasury. The producers on the prairies have to contend with a wide spread between the prices they receive for their livestock and poultry products and the prices paid to producers, for example, in the province of Ontario. The government should consider an extension of freight assistance

in order to narrow the spread on such commodities as cattle and eggs as between those paid on the prairies and in Ontario.
This item is directed to providing feed grains to farmers in central Canada and elsewhere in the nation at prices more comparable to those received and paid on the prairies. It is a good principle and I believe that the prairie producers are fully justified in asking the government to take steps to reduce the outrageous spread between the prices paid to producers on the prairies and those paid in other parts of Canada by the consumer.
I wish to make it abundantly clear that this is no criticism of the level of prices that obtain elsewhere in Canada. I am not suggesting that they may be too high in parts of Canada outside the prairies. As a matter of fact, with the government's recent policy the prices paid to producers across Canada on many products have been substantially lowered.
Measures such as those envisaged in this item represent the kind of instrument the government can use to eliminate the wide spread between prices received by western producers of such commodities as cattle, hogs, eggs and poultry and the prices received by other Canadian farmers.
This is a substantial item of great benefit to producers across Canada. We are happy to support it but we think the government should take similar action to reduce the spread in price for other agricultural commodities in an effort to meet the price now being paid for those commodities outside the prairie provinces.

Contributions to the governments of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, of one half the amounts paid by the governments of those provinces to farmers in respect of unharvested crops to a maximum of $300 in respect of any one farm; and to authorize, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, contributions to the governments of those provinces (or their municipalities) in respect of the administrative costs incurred by them in making such payments to farmers, $6,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, it might be of assistance to hon. members if I were to make a statement at the beginning of the discussion on this vote. Therefore, I will outline what has happened as far as this matter is concerned.
This vote provides for the contribution to the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba of one half of the payments made by those provinces to farmers on account of unharvested crops. The programs under which these payments are made are provincial
Supply-Agriculture
programs and are administered by the provinces. I should like to emphasize that fact. They are provincial programs, differing in each province and are administered by the provinces in each case. The dominion government, however, stipulated certain basic provisions which would be a condition of federal assistance.
Those conditions were that only farmers who had harvested less than 50 per cent of their crops were to be eligible for assistance with the maximum unharvested acreage of cereals on which payment could be made being 200 acres. The maximum payment would be $3 per acre for cereals and $600 per farm for specialty crops. Within these broad limitations the provinces were free to develop their own specific programs. This is what they did, of course, and in each province the program is somewhat different. I think perhaps I should outline what the program is in each province so that hon. members may be aware of these differences.
The program in Manitoba is as follows:
1.	There are two rates of payment based on the amount of crop a farmer has harvested.
2.	For wheat, oats, barley, flax, soybeans, navy beans, peas and rape the payments are $3 or $2 per unharvested acre, to a maximum of 200 acres.
If the amount of wheat harvested averages 5 bushels or less for each acre seeded, the payment is $3 per acre. If it is between 5 and 8 bushels the payment is $2 per acre. There is no payment if a farmer has harvested more than 8 bushels per seeded acre unless the grade is below No. 5 northern. If it is below that grade, the $2 per acre payment applies on yields up to 12 bushels per seeded acre. For other crops the yields are adjusted to a wheat equivalent.
3.	For potatoes, sugar beets and vegetables, the payment is $30 per unharvested acre to a maximum of 20 acres if less than 30 per cent of the acreage has been harvested. If between 30 per cent and 50 per cent has been harvested, the payment is $20 per acre.
In Saskatchewan, if a farmer has harvested 5| bushels of wheat or less for each acre seeded the basic payment is $3 per acre of unharvested crop. If the farmer has harvested between 5.6 and 10 bushels for each acre seeded the basic payment is $2 per acre.
There is no payment if the farmer has harvested more than 10 bushels per seeded acre. The basic payments apply only to farmers who have threshed not more than 110 acres. They are reduced progressively if more than 110 acres have been threshed. I have a table showing how much is paid for each bracket, from 111 to 120, 121 to 130 and so on. Generally speaking it can be summed

up in this way, that up to 5.5 bushels harvested per seeded acre the payments run from $3 down to 30 cents an acre and for a return of 5.6 to 10 bushels harvested per seeded acre the payments run from a maximum of $2 down to 20 cents an acre. I would ask permission, Mr. Chairman, to have this table put on Hansard, if I may.

Saskatchewan will also make payments on vetgetable crops, including potatoes, where the acreage is not less than 10 acres.
In Alberta the scheme is as follows-
In the case of oats and alfalfa is there any limitation on the payments at all?

No. With respect to oats or barley the equivalent of 10 bushels of wheat or five bushels of wheat, whichever happens to apply, is taken. I have not the figures here as to what these equivalents are but there would be roughly twice as many bushels of oats and one and a half times as many bushels of barley or something along that line.
Are the formulas more or less the same in each of the provinces?

Yes, they are. The provinces are all using the same formula for the equivalent number of bushels of barley, oats, etc. This is the scheme for Alberta. The payments apply to acreage seeded to wheat, oats, barley, rye, rapeseed and flax. When a farmer has harvested five bushels or less of

wheat for each acre seeded, the payment is $3 per unharvested acre to a maximum of 200 acres.
That is the same as Manitoba.

Yes. If the amount harvested is between five and 10 bushels of wheat per seeded acre, the payment is $2 per acre. There is no payment if the amount harvested exceeds 10 bushels of wheat per seeded acre. For other crops the yields are converted to a wheat equivalent.
I think it can be seen from this that the systems in effect in Manitoba and Alberta are fairly similar. The system in Saskatchewan varies quite a bit from the ones in effect in Manitoba and Alberta, but the Alberta and Manitoba schemes are not exactly the same. The Manitoba scheme has a provision for vegetables and things of that sort while the Alberta scheme has not, and also for those grades of wheat below No. 5, which the Alberta scheme does not include.
On that point, I do not think the minister indicated whether Saskatchewan also has any reference to the grades.
No.
At the cut-off point.

No. That outline gives some idea of the systems followed in the three provinces and the differences between them. The procedure followed by the three provinces in administering the programs also varies. In Alberta and Saskatchewan the applications from farmers for payments are dealt with first by the municipal councils, which may recommend approval or rejection. There is provision also for the councils to engage inspectors to inspect the farms of the applicants where they consider it advisable. The applications, with the recommendations of the municipal councils, then go to the provincial government for final decision and payment. The province, if it wishes, may arrange also for an inspection of any applications.
In Manitoba the applications are received at municipal offices. The municipalities, however, make no appraisal of the applications. They merely forward them to the province for handling.
I should add in this connection that the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is making available to the provinces the details of all inspections which its inspectors have made on farms from which applications for the acreage payments are received. In other words, the records we have as a result of inspections made under P.F.A.A. are made

available to the provinces so that they know what the bushel return for these farmers is. Of course, that would make it unnecessary for them to re-inspect. The processing of applications for acreage payments is now well under way.
As at February 1 Saskatchewan had approved 14,103 applications representing payment of $4,354,000. About 12,000 cheques had been issued as of that date. The province estimates that the total number of claims will be in the order of 16,000. The closing date for applications was January 30.
The Alberta government has now received close to 5,000 applications which have had preliminary processing by the municipalities. The first payment cheques will probably go out next week. Alberta expects to make a total of 10,000 payments. The closing date for applications is February 29.
In Manitoba applications for acreage payments had to be received by January 23. There are approximately 4,000 applications which are now being processed and inspections carried out. My latest information from Manitoba is that the first payment cheques will be issued by the end of this week. That, Mr. Chairman, is an outline of the scheme as it is being applied in the three provinces and a short outline of the methods being used to make the payments, in other words, the administration of the scheme.

May I ask a question before the minister resumes his seat? He gave an estimated cost of some $4,354,000 for Saskatchewan. I believe that was related to the applications in process to date. Does he have comparable figures for Manitoba and Alberta?

No, Mr. Chairman, and that was not an estimate. That was the actual amount of the payments which had been approved as of February 1. The last report we had from Saskatchewan was that they had approved the payment of $4,354,000.
Of which you will pay half.
Of which we will pay half after this vote has been passed by the house.
You have no estimate for Manitoba or Alberta?
No.

The committee will realize, of course, that we felt that the

Would the hon. member like me to answer that right now?
Yes.

This statement, to which the hon. member has just referred, was put out in error. The P.F.A.A. organization has not done and is not doing any inspections in any of the three prairie provinces. What we are doing, as I indicated, is that we make the

information we have available from the inspections we have conducted to the provinces for any farm for which they request it and for which we have records available. We are glad to get that information. There is a second point in connection with P.F.A.A., and here again we have had to depend entirely on what we read in the press on these matters. Then I find that a statement was made in Manitoba that anyone who received P.F.A.A. benefits would not be eligible for anything under this formula. The same situation applies with respect to growers of special crops. I believe that some additional information is desirable. I should like to see if I understand the information we have from the minister now. If I understand it correctly, in Manitoba and Saskatchewan there is some form of assistance provided with respect to vegetable crops. In Alberta, there is nothing provided for the growers of vegetable crops.
Not as far as I know.

Not so far as the minister knows. Then, the minister will be well aware that when the proposal was advanced there were requests from several sources to the Prime Minister when he visited his own province over the Christmas season that perhaps the deadline date for estimating the percentage of damage was not satisfactory. I wonder if there has been any adjustment in that respect? I understand the Prime Minister indicated he would consider some flexibility in that respect, too.
Well, Mr. Chairman-
Before the minister replies-

If I may just reply to these two questions; I am not quite clear as to

what the last question was. The hon. member said the Prime Minister indicated there would be some flexibility, and I was not sure what was meant.
The date on which an estimate would be made as to whether or not the unthreshed grain was under or over the 50 per cent formula.

In connection with that latter point, Mr. Chairman, there were requests made by some farmers, some municipalities and I think some farm union locals, that the date be set back to November 1. I believe it is that to which the hon. member is referring. The date of December 15 was set as a result of consultation between myself and the three ministers of agriculture of the prairie provinces. There was no argument over the date. It was mutually acceptable. It was set as December 15 because it was apparent that determination of what should be paid could not be made before December 15. If you attempted to set a date such as November 1, it would be absolutely impossible to determine how much threshing each farmer had done and in many cases the farmer himself would not be sure. It was expected, and it actually happened, that there would be a good deal of threshing done after November 1.
It was thought the fairest thing to do would be to set the date at December 15, after which time it was practically certain very little threshing, if any, would be done. This was the reason for the date of December 15. The reason the proposal to make it November 1 was not, I think, considered seriously by the provinces was the real impossibility of determining how much threshing had been done at that time when you are trying to determine it six weeks or two months later.
In so far as the other question is concerned, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked as to whether the receipt of prairie farm assistance payments would make an applicant ineligible to receive payments under this scheme. This is a matter which is entirely in the hands of the provinces. We have laid down no provision along that line. The provinces were, I know, talking about doing it, but whether or not they finally did I do not know. As far as we were concerned, there was no provision made along that line.

This item is in the estimates because of the very severe weather conditions last fall, as a result of which hundreds of thousands of acres of grain were covered by snow to the point where harvesting became impossible. As I understand the

position taken by the three prairie governments, and the Minister of Agriculture will correct me if I am wrong, they made a united submission requesting the federal government to consider this national emergency and asking the federal government to bear the whole of the cost. In addition to making that general proposition, the government was asked to make prairie farm assistance available on an individual basis and to consider unharvested crops as being no yield for the purpose of prairie farm assistance which would make many more farmers eligible for prairie farm assistance.
If this suggestion had been followed it would have meant, of course, that the government would have considered this to be essentially a national emergency, that the federal government itself would be dealing with it and would be paying the moneys from the national treasury in order to meet this national emergency.
I think there is a growing feeling in all of the provinces in Canada that the provision of matching grants from the federal government for a huge variety of projects, if extended almost beyond limit, removes the control of provincial revenues from the hands of the provinces. Before any joint scheme is entered into I think there should be the greatest amount of consultation and agreement with the provinces. As I understand this particular item, there was consultation and there was discussion but the announcement was made by the federal government and the provinces then could take it or leave it or could enter into negotiations to vary the method by which it was applied.
Prairie farm assistance is not a charge on the provincial treasury of any province. The minister has not been able to give us today sufficient information to enable us to determine how the cost of this scheme will be apportioned amongst the three prairie provinces. He did not have sufficient information. But we know the general division of agriculture in the three prairie provinces. The chances are that Saskatchewan will be paying the largest amount, followed by Alberta, followed by Manitoba with a much smaller amount. Saskatchewan being the main agricultural province in the sense that it has a larger agricultural acreage than either Alberta or Manitoba, it follows that in any scheme of matching grants it will bear an undue share of the burden.
These are some of the reasons why I feel as I do about a scheme which says to the provinces, "If your people are going to qualify for payment, then you must put
Supply-Agriculture
up half of the cost". I think the government's federal-provincial relations have not always been good. As far as this question is concerned, there was some prior consultation but this was following a very bitter experience, as far as the provinces are concerned, with the government's attitude toward crop insurance in that the government merely made the announcement saying that the federal government would pay 20 per cent of the cash premium cost and the provinces would be responsible, along with the producers in the province for the other 80 per cent. These kinds of projects, if carried on at great length, will disrupt federal-provincial relations in this country because such action will make it impossible for provincial governments to have sufficient revenue to carry on the projects under their jurisdiction and which they feel should be done for the people of that province.
The Saskatchewan government, as far as I have been able to ascertain, have always been most co-operative with the present administration and with the former administration. I think that is a laudable position for the Saskatchewan government to take. I am certain that this government has found-as the former administration at times said it found-Saskatchewan very easy to deal with in these joint projects. However, that consideration does not detract from the statement I made that legislation such as this dealing with a national emergency should, in my opinion, be legislation that is primarily federal in character, where the federal government bears the largest proportion of the cost if not all of it.
Farmers are not going to receive huge sums of money. When we were in a debate on another subject on another occasion, Mr. Chairman, when an amount of a dollar an acre was involved up to $200, I called it peanuts. I think it was peanuts as far as the individual producer was concerned and that it was peanuts in relation to the cost of farming and in relation to the need farmers have for a larger income. The total that can be involved in this estimate for any one farmer is $600. The sum of $600 payable to a producer will be of some definite advantage, without question.
Certainly one of the important reasons that weather conditions brought about this emergency on the prairies is the extremely difficult income position in which prairie producers find themselves. This extremely difficult income position which requires action along these lines has resulted from the government's failure to solve the farmers' basic economic problem and the price-cost squeeze. As far as the farmers are concerned, this government seems to take a differing attitude,

.depending upon the item under discussion. When it comes to acreage payments, the government is very much in favour of the little person, the small operator. But the .other day, in the operation of another agri-,cultural policy, we found that as far as the small business operator is concerned, the government could not care less whether he [DOT]went out of business. The minister was not interested in co-operating so that deficiency payments would be made in the case of hogs that were slaughtered and the small butcher [DOT]could remain in business. But even for a large producer, the payments that are provided under this item will be welcome.
Some people feel that the farmers in western Canada are making very large sums of money, and that on a relatively small investment they can make a good living. I think it was the hon. member for Jasper-Edson who last year in this house made his famous statement in which he said he was opposed to deficiency payments because it would merely mean that a farmer who was driving a Cadillac would then be able to drive only a Buick. I think it was one of the most regrettable statements that has ever been made by a western member. I think the hon. member for Jasper-Edson might take a leaf out of the book of the hon. member :for Rosthern who made such a thoughtful .and constructive speech in this house the other day-
Oh, oh.
-in which he so ably and so diligently exposed the government's agricultural policy for just what it is.

I understand the chairman is saying order. I think it is a rather touchy subject with people other than the chairman. Therefore, they are bringing it to the attention of the chairman.
I was talking about the price-cost squeeze and the very difficult income position in western Canada which turns the bad weather conditions into what is in fact, that is, a grave emergency. The interprovincial farm unions council made a submission on November 23 to the federal-provincial agriculture conference, and I think they pointed out very well the difficult position in which farmers on the prairie now find themselves. They pointed out that in a given farm management survey, the group of farms which was investigated had an average capital investment of $55,000; that after having set aside $3,000 as an appropriate amount for farm labour and income for the farmer and his family, the net return on the capital investment was 1.2 per cent. A $55,000 investment would suggest to me a

relatively good sized farm, a relatively efficient farm; and on a farm such as this, after a moderate amount has been retained for family labour income of just $250 a month, the net return on the investment was 1.2 per cent. In other words, from the standpoint of business accounting, western agriculture is in an exceedingly difficult position and, from a cost accounting standpoint at any rate, would be considered near bankruptcy. With a situation like that, even amongst the relatively well-to-do farmers this action now being taken, this minimal action, is very much in order.
I think there are other things the government should be doing to supplement this item, and I had thought that perhaps an announcement would be made in this house by this time about the interim payment on wheat, oats and barley. The Minister of Trade and Commerce on Monday, January 18, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Melville, said that an announcement would be made, I believe he said within a week, but certainly by the end of the month, and that this was earlier action than had been taken by the former administration. I think it is high time that the Minister of Trade and Commerce together with his colleague the Minister of Agriculture, saw to it that these payments were made and put in the hands of the producers, because they would be of some advantage to producers who are in a difficult position owing to harvesting conditions on the prairies.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, when we were discussing the cash advance legislation and the guaranteed bank loans legislation the other day, there was another field of appropriate action that the government should follow which would help relieve the financial situation that is covered by this estimate. I refer to the whole question of deficiency payments and the necessity for the government to make a decision on this matter and to inform the house of just what the decision is. We would be in a much better position today to discuss the financial need of the prairie producers if we knew whether or not the government would pay the producers money as a result of other requests that have been made. The farmers' agricultural position is worsening, and-

Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to raise a point of order, but the hon. member is making a general agricultural speech. He is well aware of the fact that the estimates for this year have now been tabled in the house, and that discussion of these estimates, including those of agriculture, will be coming on, and that is the time to make a general agricultural speech. This particular item provides

the dominion government's share of a form of relief assistance which has been given to a limited number of farmers in western Canada, and I submit it is not in order for the hon. member, as he has been doing, to make a general speech on agriculture dealing with all branches of agriculture. If he does so, there is no reason why every other hon. member of this house should not make a similar type of speech. When we are dealing with the regular estimates for agriculture, you, sir, and all hon. members of this house are aware of the fact that the general discussion of agriculture always goes on for several days. Sometimes it has gone on for two weeks, but it always goes on for several days. When we are dealing with the dominion government's share of payments, really of a relief nature, to a limited number of farmers in western Canada, I do not think it is appropriate or in order to make general speeches on agriculture.
I would appeal to the hon. member to recognize the fairness and rightness of the points I have just made, because I certainly think it would be quite wrong for us to go on here for several days with a general discussion on agriculture, and that is what the type of speech the hon. member is making will inevitably lead to.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word on this point of order. I was listening most attentively to the hon. member for Athabasca, and he-
Not attentively enough, It seems.

I mean Assiniboia; I
apologize for the confusion in my mind. However, I have no confusion in my mind about the point I wish to make. The hon. member for Assiniboia was saying that if we knew what the government was going to do about something else, we would be able to make a better judgment as to whether we should spend the taxpayers' money on this. If this committee is to be so restricted that we cannot say what kind of information we think we ought to have before we vote the taxpayers' money, I can see no purpose in having a committee of supply at all. Surely that is the most fundamental function which this parliament has. What the minister is suggesting is, of course, just what the attitude of the government has been over the whole question, that they should do what they like and treat us as a rubber stamp.

On the point of order which has been raised, Mr. Chairman, on reflection I think you will agree with me that I am very much in order. I have been talking about the income position of the farmers on the
Supply-Agriculture
prairies related to the income position of the very farmers that are affected by this legislation. We are being asked to vote a sum of $6 million for a specific purpose, and I am suggesting that, under the set of agricultural conditions which now exist, in order to deal with this emergency this amount of money should be much higher. In order to make any fair' assessment of whether or not it is adequate, we require the type of information I have requested, and I think this is very much to the point.
I do not know why the Minister of Agriculture is so sensitive. I do not know why he is trying to enforce a closure on discussion of this item. I do not know why he wants to restrict unduly the debate on this item. If I had been talking about conditions all across Canada, I think I would be out of order; but I was talking about the economic conditions of the very producers that this item covers, and whether or not this item, in light of those economic conditions, is adequate, and I contend I am very much in order.

Mr. Chairman, I think you will realize that the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, and in the latter part of his remarks the hon. member for Assiniboia, were not directing themselves to the point of order I raised at all. They were both making purely political speeches designed to create an incorrect impression, particularly outside this chamber. There has been no effort whatever to try to curtail discussion which is relevant to the matter which is under consideration. The point I have in mind, and with which neither of these hon. members dealt, is that this is an item for a specific purpose and that a general discussion on agriculture, agricultural income conditions, deficiency payments and so forth, which is proper when the first item of the general estimates for the year is discussed, is not proper and in order at this point.

I can understand the difficulty in which the Minister of Agriculture finds himself. However, I think that if he were to have posed for himself this question: would the farmers of western Canada- the three provinces concerned-have needed this particular assistance if the government had acted favourably on the request made by the farmers-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for his observations. I have been listening very carefully to the hon. member for Assiniboia and there were times when I think he was trying to make a basis of comparison; but I do think he strayed considerably from this item and I would ask him to return to it and try to follow it more closely.

I think I was speaking very much on this item and that the remarks I was trying to make were very pertinent to this question. I was about to point out that one of the reasons why an item like this is necessary is because of the worsening agricultural picture for the farmers who are involved. I do not have to quote anyone other than the Minister of Agriculture himself who has pointed out that the index of prices of goods and services which are used by these farmers showed an increase in 1959 of 3.1 per cent as compared with the previous year. This is one of the factors which contribute 
toward making this item necessary. This has nothing to do with weather conditions as such. If the farmers were getting the kind of agricultural deal they should be getting from this government, the emergency which followed from weather conditions would be relatively light compared with the emergency which results from the general agricultural picture.
I understand that one of the leading farm spokesmen made a statement the other day that conditions are so bad now in parts of northern Alberta that farmers are taking wheat 150 miles to a grist mill to have it milled into flour because they are so short of cash.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am not sure how the hon. member can relate those remarks to this item. As I understand this item it is to pay for wheat lost because of the snow.
We do not know that it is lost.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We do not know it is lost, but that is the assumption. This item is not designed to aid farmers all over the country. Those whose crops were not snowed under will not participate.

Surely, the economic picture of the producers involved has something to do with this amount and I contend that if farmers are so destitute financially that in order to get enough flour for the winter they have to take their grain 150 miles to have it ground into flour, then this item is far too low.
This is unthreshed grain. Stick to the point.

I notice that whenever one is advocating something in this house that is very much needed and necessary to the welfare of the people we represent, and if there should be any suggestion or criticism of the government, then we hear great rumblings from the government seats. I think hon. gentlemen opposite should have the patience to hear one of us who is speaking without these frequent interruptions. The Prime Minister lectured parliament this morning about waste and frivolity. I think he might have turned around and lectured some of the people who sit behind him.
Order.

As much as the Prime Minister was out of order at the time he spoke.

As I was saying, the general economic conditions on the prairies makes

this item far too small to relieve the financial position of the farmers who are experiencing difficulty because their crops are under snow. They came to this government in time of emergency. They asked the government to act, and the government has acted by asking the provinces to bear half the cost and by including this item in the estimates allowing payments up to a maximum of $3 an acre. One of the leading spokesmen for the western farmers made a statement the other day, I understand, and I am quite sure that this legislation is one of the reasons why he made the statement. He said there is more irritation on the prairies with this government today than with any other government at any time since the hungry thirties.

speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member for Assiniboia but I am obliged to advise him that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order to which I started to speak, surely when the committee is discussing an item of this nature we do not have to listen to a political tirade of five minutes' duration that has no relevance whatever to this item.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, and further to the insulting remark of the minister, I know that the hon. gentleman is very sensitive to any criticism of the government and the Prime Minister, but I would suggest to him through you, sir, that you are quite capable of rising as you did on occasion if you consider me out of order in the remarks I am making. I do not think we have to listen to a lecture from the Minister of Agriculture after my time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make just a few brief remarks on this item and I can assure you that they will be relevant. First of all I should like to refer to the remarks I made on a previous occasion when we were discussing aid to western farmers

Supply-Agriculture
as those remarks appear at page 175 of Hansard of January 21, 1960:
-I would like to say that in my opinion it would have been better had the joint assistance between the provinces and the federal government been paid on all unharvested acreage to the maximum of 200 acres.
I should like to ask the minister if he would tell us on what basis the decision was made to pay on unharvested acreage under 50 per cent. In 1959 western Canada experienced three and one half months of extremely wet weather. Many farmers made an effort between storms and at every opportunity to harvest the crops which they did resulting in a good many cases, particularly with respect to small farmers, in their completing the harvesting of over 50 per cent of their grain. This grain is difficult to store and handle for feed and is extremely restricted as to movement because of the limited facilities for drying the grain.
The small farmer with 49 per cent of his grain harvested is left without assistance. He suffers undue hardship because no assistance is available to him until the spring when he can harvest the balance of his crop and thus perhaps qualify for prairie farm assistance if his yield is low. I should like to have the minister tell us on what basis the decision was made to pay assistance on unharvested grain under 50 pear cent?
Before I resume my seat I should like to say to the hon. member for Essex East that I would be pleased to have him spend the period of the next recess in my constituency so that he could learn something about western agriculture at close and first hand.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with keen interest to what the hon. member for Assiniboia had to say as he unveiled what I thought at first must be the new agricultural platform of the new party with its distinguishing characteristic of the promise of milk and honey. It seems however to bear all the characteristics of the same old tattered, torn and unsupportable planks we have heard before. I think the best way to describe it is in words Sir Winston Churchill once used: "A sheep in sheep's clothing."
I want to commend in the highest possible terms the principle inherent in this estimate which the committee is now considering. I do so not only because I realize it will be of great benefit to many farmers in western Canada where I have seen it in operation but, taking it in reverse, I saw at first hand what could happen-and I think this is most important

when this type of assistance is rejected.
In 1957 in my constituency of Peace River there was a disaster of far greater magni-

tude than that experienced by western Canada last year. In 1957 I believe approximately 70 per cent of the crops in that great country were lost by reason of weather conditions including rain, snow, frost and all the vicissitudes that can be experienced. As a result the farmers, municipal groups and farm organizations combined and sent a committee to Edmonton to attempt to communicate with the provincial and federal governments.
I remember that well because one of the leaders of that delegation who was a Liberal at the time came to me afterwards and said they had sent a wire to the present federal Minister of Agriculture and he was amazed at receiving a reply within two hours. He said that this was the first time he realized there had been a change in government. They had requested some assistance for the people affected by this disaster which was of such magnitude. The federal government took the position that constitutionally it was essential that the provincial government should first declare that there was a disaster before the federal government could help with the situation and contribute financially.
Unfortunately at that time the Alberta government was engaged in the very interesting pastime of paying out some $12 million in what they called oil royalty dividends. They have been called other names but that was the description. They were thus in the embarrassing position of finding it utterly impossible to say that they did not have the financial ability to deal with the situation and consequently could not ask the federal government to intervene. In the result, so far as my part of the country is concerned, we lost approximately 70 per cent of the crop, and the people of that area are only just recovering from that disaster.
The federal government stood prepared then, as it does now, to come to the assistance of our people. It is only through the fault and neglect of the provincial government of Alberta that that was not done then.
Where are all these points of order experts now?

As a matter of fact, I have some press clippings here indicating that the Alberta government persisted in its attitude. I have one here from the Regina Leader-Post of December 2, 1959, headed, "Alberta Says No". The Alberta government had indicated at that time its refusal to accept the offer of the federal government, an offer which is being implemented by legislation we have already passed and through this item.

We find that after December 3 the provincial governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan indicated that, with some modifications, they would accept the proposal which apparently had been advanced by the federal government. Consequently, in due course the Alberta government was driven into acceptance of the proposal, and in my opinion that is the only reason why they have accepted the offer and why this item now applies to them.
I think that is sufficient to indicate the importance of passing this estimate. Without it we would find that many farmers throughout western Canada would be in very unfortunate circumstances. I commend the immediate rapid passage of the estimate for the payment of these funds and suggest that they will serve a very useful purpose.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be quite brief and in order. I rise first of all to express my support for this item and to say that we are very pleased to know that the prairie grain producers who require this money are getting even this measure of assistance. But I also rose to ask the minister a simple question, although I see he is behind the curtain at the moment. I was really waiting for him. In my constituency and in other parts of British Columbia the cherry growers lost 50 per cent of their crop on account of the weather and the peach growers also lost 50 per cent of their crop on account of the weather.

No.

I was just about to ask my question.

The hon. member obviously was out of order in talking about legislation concerning only that province but there was no point of order raised when he made that statement. to conclude with his one sentence I imagine that he was about to say that this type of legislation-
Order.
should be made more universal, and I think that such a statement is wholly in order.

May I just say that I am sure that the Chairman, in giving attention to the problem as he is, is doing it with a desire to see that the rules are properly observed. But surely the observation just made by the hon. member for Assini-boia has validity when one realizes that this is the first opportunity we have had to discuss this measure in terms of a specific item before us. Normally if this measure had not been introduced by way of an estimate it would have been introduced by way of a bill. Under the rules of the house we would then have been permitted wide latitude on the first clause of the bill, a latitude that certainly would go way beyond a mere suggestion that this kind of measure might very well be adapted to meet similar situations involving disasters with regard to other crops. It is only because of my confidence in the Chairman who has occupied this position for the first time in recent days that I suggest that too strict an interpretation will preclude debate in the manner now suggested which I think is in the interests of this particular legislation.

I was simply going to ask the minister, after bringing to his attention the difficulties of some of my producers, what is behind the government's thinking that provides for assistance, which we support, for a certain group of farmers in Canada in a certain area because they have suffered losses on account of the weather and does not provide assistance for farmers in other areas who have suffered losses on account of the weather? This is an intriguing moral and ethical problem and I should like the minister to inform the house what is behind the government's thinking in this piecemeal approach to farmers' problems in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the relevant bills were discussed in committee I ruled that we could not discuss other disasters or other losses than the one to which this item has reference. I may be wrong. It may be that this is one of the first times I have occupied the chair, but that is the way I interpret the rules and that is the way I think they should apply in order to protect the rights of parliament and every individual member.

Mr. Chairman, in dealing with item 613 which has to do with contributions to the provincial governments of the prairie

Supply-Agriculture
provinces of one half the amounts paid by those governments to farmers in respect of unharvested crops to a maximum of $300 in respect of any one farm, as well as contributions with respect to the administrative costs incurred by the provinces in making such payments to farmers, may I say that I should like to commend the government for introducing this item so early in the session. The amount of $6 million, together with the $6 million which will be paid by the provinces, will not alleviate all of the distress on the farms but it certainly will be a step in the right direction, in conjunction with the other agricultural measures we have taken.
I can understand the difficulty of the C.C.F. in speaking to this item because they have only one representative from the prairies. I can understand the even greater difficulty of the Liberals who have no representatives from the prairies.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, would Your Honour indicate what this has to do with the item before us?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the point of order is well taken and I would ask the hon. member to stick to the discussion of the item. I do not think his remarks are relevant at this time.

In my remarks today I want to say a few words regarding the extent of the crops lying under snow east of the Red river and particularly in my riding of Springfield. I have before me a map compiled by the prairie farm assistance officials which sets forth the results of their inspection east of the Red river. I think the figures that I am about to give will be ample proof to demonstrate to hon. members the situation on the prairies as a whole, and in my own area in particular, and that the situation can be called disastrous.
The extent of the losses is probably one reason why these payments are being called disaster payments. There are approximately 160 townships east of the Red river which may be called agricultural. Approximately one half, or 80 of them, are in my constituency of Springfield. Of the 80 agricultural townships in my constituency approximately 60, or 75 per cent, were eligible for P.F.A.A. payments. In other words, 75 per cent of the total agricultural area had a yield of fewer than eight bushels per acre. A further breakdown of those figures shows that approximately 20 of those 60 eligible townships had a yield of zero to three bushels per acre. This represents 25 per cent of the agricultural area. Approximately ten townships had a yield of three to five bushels per acre. Thirty townships, or 50 per cent of the area, had a yield of

five to eight bushels per acre. This is an area where the average yield is around 30 bushels of wheat to the acre ordinarily.
Early in December last year the Minister of Agriculture agreed that the whole area east of the Red river should be considered as an area in which all the crops unharvested as of that date would be considered a total loss. This made it possible for the prairie farm assistance inspectors to get out into the field early and make their assessments. I should like to state that to date in my constituency over $186,000 has been paid out in prairie farm assistance payments, and by February 15 the amount will be $326,200.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I cannot relate the comments of the hon. member to the subject matter. It seems to me that the item under discussion refers only to grain unharvested because of the early snowfalls. I fail to see how the remarks of the hon. member cover the item under discussion.

I would like to explain to you, sir, that in Manitoba, under the regulations having to do with these payments, people who receive prairie farm assistance payments are not eligible for those disaster payments and, therefore, I think it has a direct bearing on the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member thinks that they should come under this item. Is that the argument he wants to make?

There has been considerable opposition in the legislature of Manitoba from the opposition regarding the fact that in Manitoba, under this disaster program, prairie farm assistance payments are not included, as they are in some of the other provinces, and I was trying to show the extent to which payments are being made in Manitoba. Also, Mr. Chairman, these are the only figures that we have available to demonstrate the extent of the crops lying under the snow in Manitoba.
As the Minister of Agriculture has already pointed out, a lot of the data which has been garnered by the inspectors of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been turned over to the provincial authorities who are using that material in their payments under the disaster payment program. Therefore, I feel it has a direct bearing. However, I am coming to the conclusion of these remarks. What I wish to say is that the amount of money which the province of Manitoba had available was such that it deemed it necessary to preclude those who have already received assistance under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act from receiving disaster payments. They felt that the money they had available would be best directed to those who could not be eligible

for any other type of assistance. In this respect I think it has already been brought out by the Minister of Agriculture that in Manitoba we are providing under this disaster payments program assistance to vegetable growers and growers of specialty crops in Manitoba.
In Manitoba it has been possible-perhaps because they did not extend the payments to those receiving prairie farm assistance-to give a more equitable payment to those who suffered losses of vegetables on which the costs incurred per acre are far greater than they are in the growing of wheat. The Minister of Agriculture has already brought out the fact that payments in Manitoba for potatoes, for instance, are $30 per acre, which is roughly the equivalent of the payment on ten acres of wheat.
In my own area we have a great number of small mixed farmers who grow wheat and vegetables as well. It has been possible under this conversion formula for them to become eligible for payments which they would not have been eligible for if the formula had been worked out strictly on an acreage basis. Most of them managed to harvest some of their crops, very early grain crops; whereas potato crops usually come in later and in this instance were lying unharvested.
In my own constituency of Springfield approximately 40 per cent of all farmers received prairie farm assistance payments with an average of $170. When we consider the amount paid last year, which was around $20,000, and compare it with $326,000 paid this year, I think the extent of the hardship of the farmers can well be imagined.
During this session we have already passed two bills which will be a measure of assistance to the farmers. I refer to the cash advances on unthreshed grain and the guaranteed farm loans. But because of the large amount of grain lying under the snow in Manitoba, particularly in eastern Manitoba, and because of the fact that the land was so wet, it is very unlikely that any of this grain will be harvested, and it is very unlikely that many of the farmers in my area will be able to take advantage of this recent cash advance legislation, when we consider that the crops have already been declared a total loss.
In concluding I should like to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Essex East to the effect that if we had accepted deficiency payments this item would not be necessary. I would merely like to point out that if the Liberal government had accepted crop insurance 20 years ago this item also would not have been necessary. While on that subject, Mr. Chairman, I should
