like to say that in the province of Manitoba, we are in the process of adopting a crop insurance scheme. I hope that in future years various phases for working out an extension of it to all farmers will be gone into so that never again will we have to bring in legislation such as this.

I simply rise to ask the minister a question that I think is germane at this point, before we proceed further with the debate. Item 613 refers to terms and conditions of an order in council. I wonder whether the minister would indicate to the committee what orders in council have been passed in connection with this item, and perhaps he would produce a copy of the order in council.

Mr. Chairman, the orders in council have been filed in the normal way for publication in the Canada Gazette. I have not brought copies of them with me. I can see if I can get copies of the orders in council, or a copy of it brought in, if the hon. member wishes. As I say, I have not it with me at the moment.
Does the minister recall the date of the order in council?
It is not mentioned here? No, I do not recall the date.
Perhaps, while the debate proceeds, one of the minister's staff would try to obtain it.
Mr. Chairman-

No, Mr. Chairman. I was rising because I thought perhaps you would hear a member of the opposition, having heard two or three members on the government side.
Oh, oh.

speechtext: Order. Even though the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River did not speak for long, I thought he was expressing the views of the opposition. I recognize the hon. member for Acadia.

I did not intend to speak on this item because I am in agreement with it. But after listening to the hon. member for Assiniboia carry on in his speech, one which consisted of nothing but political blabbering and made not for the benefit of this house but for his constituents and those in Saskatchewan who follow him-

I am rising on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I have no objection to being passed over in favour of the hon. gentleman if he is going to speak on the item before the committee. But if the hon. gentleman is going to take advantage of the situation in order to abuse some other hon. member, I think he should be called to order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was going to give the hon. member for Acadia a chance to make his introductory remarks and I was sure that he was coming to the point.

I thank the Chair very much. These were my introductory remarks. I did intend to speak quite clearly and quite to the point on item 613. As I said, the hon. member for Assiniboia was doing nothing but making political blabbering for the benefit of those followers of his in Saskatchewan, not for the benefit of the house.
I was trying to help the farmers.

The hon. member
interrupts. He does not like it. His skin is thin. He went on to point out that we were objecting to his speech when at one time all that one hon. member said was "that is not so", or something to that effect. Then he paused. He had a word or two to say about interruptions. He wondered who was making the rumblings. He wanted it down in print so that it would look good, so that it would appear that this house is trying to quelch the remarks he was trying to make. He spoke for half an hour and took up probably three quarters of an hour with interruptions, all a bunch of political blabberings the like of which I have never heard before.
Then the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River went on to speak about three relief measures. Three relief measures were not brought in. The first two measures had nothing to do with relief. They dealt with cash advances and farm loans which have to be paid back by the farmers and they certainly cannot be termed relief measures. Let us just clear that matter up.
Then some remark was made by the same hon. member about the P.F.A.A. payments and he wondered whether there would be overlapping. In the northern part of the province the crops are not even off in one area. Maybe less than 10 per cent of the acreage is off. How can P.F.A.A. payments be made on those crops until spring? They cannot be made until that crop is harvested. Therefore there may well be overlapping. I cannot see how there cannot be because this payment was going to be to those whose crops are more than 50 per cent still out and the P.F.A.A. surveys cannot be made

until the crop is harvested. Apparently there seems to be a great lack of understanding on the opposite side of the house.
Then the hon. member for Assiniboia went on at great length and tried to compare this measure with deficiency payments and to say that if deficiency payments had been paid, this measure would not be necessary. Let me tell hon. members of this house that in many of the circumstances this benefit will go out to the northern part of the province and deficiency payments would have had little effect in the northern part of the province on the financial wealth of those farmers. Let us just clear up that matter.
Then I should like to point out that the hon. member for Assiniboia went on to speak as though this $2 million or $3 million that was coming out of the Saskatchewan government was coming out of his own pocket. He seemed to be quite worried about it. May I say this to him? If this federal government had not gone ahead with this item 613, the provincial governments, including his own in Saskatchewan, would have given the farmers not a ruddy penny. This government is bringing in a measure to pay the farmers $6 million and the provinces are going to pay another $6 million so that, under a true evaluation of the benefit of this act, the farmers of western Canada are going to gain $12 million, as a result mainly of action by this government. Speaking as a farmer in western Canada, I do not particularly care which government it comes out of, as long as it comes into the farmer's pockets. I am not too worried about the Alberta government running out of money and I am not too worried about the provincial government of the hon. member's province, namely Saskatchewan, running out of money. However, I am worried about the farmers in those provinces running out of money, and that is my biggest concern.
The hon. member went on to say that he listened to the farm representatives. Yet when the last farm representative was speaking, he was not listening to him at all. He was carrying on a private caucus over in that far corner of the chamber. He was not listening to the hon. member who was speaking. Yet he says, "I listened to the farm representatives."

I listened to the important
ones.
The hon. member interrupts me. Let him go ahead and do so. He does not like what I am saying. He has a tendency to listen to those farm representatives to whom he wants to listen, and that is all.

Mr. Chairman, I think there is one point made by the hon. gentleman

who has just taken his seat with which I am forced to agree. When he said there was a lack of understanding of this measure, I think he did not exaggerate the situation. To find the reason for that lack of understanding one does not have to seek far. Lest you think I am not going to talk about the item, I intend to read it. It reads as follows:
Contributions to the governments of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, of one half the amounts paid by the governments of those provinces to farmers in respect of unharvested crops to a maximum of $300 in respect of any one farm: and to authorize, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council, contributions to the governments of those provinces (or their municipalities) in respect of the administrative costs incurred by them in making such payments to farmers-
If that language means anything, it means that certain orders in council have been passed by a government headed by a gentleman who denounced government by order in council in season and out of season from the time he came into this parliament in 1940 until the day he began to occupy a treasury bench. But when my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River rises in his place and asks the minister if he will read the order in council which prescribes the terms on which this money belonging to the taxpayers of Canada is to be paid out, the minister says, "Oh, that was published in the Canada Gazette but I have not a copy of it here. I do not see any particular reason why parliament should have it but I will send for it if the hon. member wants it".
That is not true.
Mr. Chairman-
You are against the western farmers.

speechtext: Order.

When the hon. and distinguished member from northern Alberta who has just been expressing himself with such great courtesy has concluded, I will continue, Mr. Chairman.
What I was saying was that from the beginning to the end of this operation, so far as this parliament is concerned, that is the attitude this government has taken. In the speech from the throne we were told that certain legislation was to be brought in to deal with an emergency which we and the hon. gentlemen who sit in the corner of the chamber there both recognized was an emergency and with which we both agreed without any hesitation the government should have priority to deal before the continuation of the speech from the throne.

We both expected and had every right to expect from the language used in the speech from the throne that legislation would be brought in first about the main thing and then about the subsidiary things. No legislation was forthcoming. During the debate on those subsidiary measures an effort was made to make it as difficult as possible for us to get any information about what the government was doing. Then we were told that money was actually being spent out of the treasury of one of the provinces that we were later going to be asked to vote money to recoup.
I say that that is no way for any government to treat a free parliament. That is no way to treat a free parliament, to bring in an estimate worded in this fashion without any details of how the money is being spent. We are expected to swallow this this language which gives no description whatsoever.
Now, not only that, but the house has been misled, or certainly I have been misled-
That is easy enough.

As the hon. member says, I am very easily misled because I have been in the habit in the past of taking the word of ministers of the crown at its face value. Yet we were told in this house by the Prime Minister, in response to a question I asked, that no agreement had been made with any of the provincial governments, though we were told by the Minister of Agriculture that assurances had been given to them, albeit we have never been told what they were. We are expected to take that on faith.
I have in my hand a copy of the debates of the Manitoba legislature for Thursday, January 28, and I would like to read this short extract which deals precisely with this measure now before us.

Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I would like permission to direct a question to the hon. the Minister of Agriculture. Did the Manitoba government receive a commitment, verbal or written, that the federal government will pay half of the cost of the Emergency Assistance Program?

-
That is the minister of agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure as to what the hon. member from Gladstone means, but at the present time we have a verbal agreement with Ottawa that the program which has been approved of by the government of Manitoba will be met on a 50-50 basis, provincial and federal.

A subsequent question, Mr. Speaker, in view of the answer given. I wonder if the hon. the minister, Mr. Speaker, could explain why the Prime Minister of Canada in the House of Commons yesterday indicated in reply to a question that no such commitment has yet been given?

I wouldn't have the slightest idea of why the Prime Minister of Canada would make that remark-

I happened to be in the gallery of the Manitoba legislature that day and heard this exchange take place. I was astonished, because there we had the minister of agriculture, a minister of the crown in the province, saying there is a verbal agreement with this government, and I had understood the Prime Minister to have said in this house the day before in response to my question that there was no commitment of any kind. Whether "agreement" or "commitment" are different things in the language of this government, they were not different things in the language of the last government or any other government in the history of this country.
Then what do we get from the Prime Minister? We get from the Prime Minister, when I asked him on Monday last, this interesting statement. I do not want to go over all this stuff, but on page 546 of Hansard for February 1 he said:
Mr. Speaker, may I say to the hon. gentleman that it is difficult to understand a question such as that.
That is the question I asked.
He has been given the answer that no agreement was entered into with any of the provinces.
The minister of agriculture in Manitoba, who is a young man and struck me, from looking at him, as being a very sincere, simple, straightforward fellow-
Capable.

The hon. member says capable, and I would also think truthful. The minister of agriculture of Manitoba said that they have a verbal agreement, but on the following Monday the Prime Minister of this country says there is no agreement. In other words, the minister of agriculture of Manitoba was lying to the legislature of Manitoba. That is the only possible inference that anyone can draw from what happened in this house last Monday.

He-

-has been given the answer that no agreement was entered into with any of the provinces.

speechtext: The hon. member has given the answer completely out of context. Read the entire answer.

Are you talking the bill out?

In committee we can speak for as long as we like, as we were taught by hon. members who used to sit over here not so very long ago, and who will be sitting over here before very long. I will read my first question, as reported at page 546 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government has given any other assurances-
In using the word "assurances", I was referring to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture that assurances had been given to the prairie governments, and those assurances were-if the minister thinks I am being unfair he can correct me instantly- that this matter would be brought before this parliament. The question I asked was:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government has given any other assurances to any provincial governments to share in expenditures made by those governments which

have not been communicated to parliament and, if so, when the government intends to communicate such assurances to parliament.

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, I believe I have the floor.

That does not happen to be correct.
-there is no argument about it.

The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate and other hon. members in the Liberal party have been making a great fuss over the fact that this assistance was being given, or at least over the fact that assurances were being given to the western farmers, without the matter first having been brought up in parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. That is a complete misrepresentation of my position as the hon. member knows perfectly well. I said we had no objection to assurances but they should have been brought to parliament at the first opportunity and not a month later.

On that point, Mr. Chairman, I draw the minister's attention to the past tense used in the language of the item. It is not "to be prescribed" but "prescribed."

It may be that the tense used is not correct and I would not argue that matter but I did not want to have persist any longer than possible the false impression that the order in council had been passed. I was eager to clear up that matter.
The hon. member for Assiniboia brought up the point that the provinces initially asked to have the dominion government pay the whole cost of this type of relief. Naturally the provinces asked the dominion government to do so and they follow this course with respect to practically every expenditure that is going to be made. I suppose it is human nature that that should be the case. However, the actual situation is that the primary responsibility for relief or assistance in a situation of this kind rests with the municipalities

and the provinces. They are primarily responsible for the assistance which is necessary in situations if of this nature.
The hon. member for Kootenay West wanted to know why we did not make payments of this same nature to farmers of every kind throughout all of Canada who may have lost their crops from any cause whatever. The answer to that is this. Where the loss of crop has taken place or a disaster has occurred in a small area it is the responsibility of the municipality and the province to relieve the distress which may result therefrom and if the relief of that distress is beyond the capability of those two bodies the province is free to apply to the dominion government for assistance in relieving the distress. That is what happened in the case of the Winnipeg flood, the Fraser river floods and in the case of the snow covered crops in western Canada on this occasion. The provinces have asked the federal government to assist. As a matter of fact, initially they asked the government to pay the whole cost of this assistance.
After discussing the matter with them we said we were agreeable to the proposition that the federal government should share in the cost of that assistance. I should like to point out that the payment of $3 an acre which is being made is an assistance payment. It is not designed, as many seem to think, to compensate farmers for the loss of their crop. It is designed to give the farmers some assistance, a small measure of compensation for the amount of loss which they will inevitably suffer as a result of the crop being under the snow during the winter.
When a crop is under the snow there is always some loss from mice and deterioration due to weather, and so forth. The $3 payment is designed to provide some measure of compensation for the inevitable loss on crops which are under the snow.

the second reading of Bill No. C-9, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (application to civil service).
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to move second reading of this bill perhaps I should outline again, even though I did so at the introductory stage, the purpose of this measure. Basically it is to provide that the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, with one or two slight exceptions, shall be applicable to the crown and to the employees of the crown, that is, to the government and to the civil service. The process of certification would apply if the bill should be passed. The provisions relating to negotiations with the civil servants and requiring the government to sit down and bargain with them if they receive certification would also apply.
The conciliation services now provided by the act to employees of private employers who come within the jurisdiction of the legislation would be available with respect to negotiations conducted between civil servants and the government except that the conciliation board proceedings would in effect be a board of arbitration. The decision of the board of arbitration, if it should be established pursuant to the bill being passed and taking its place in the statute books, would be binding upon the government and upon the employees in the public service. Those provisions of the act which the bill does not intend to make applicable to employee-employer relationships of the civil servants and the government are those sections that relate to strikes and lockouts.
Perhaps I might deal first with one argument that has been used pretty extensively, not only on previous occasions in the House of Commons when the subject matter of this bill was raised although not in bill form but also in my own home province of British Columbia where the provincial government employees have been campaigning for collective bargaining rights for quite a number of years. The answer that has been given here and in other legislative bodies from time to time when the question of granting collective bargaining rights to civil servants by making the same law applicable to them as is applicable to other employees and employers has been raised is that we would in effect be giving away what is a parliamentary right to determine what the wage or salary structure will be. It has been said that that is

not in keeping with the practice of government or the operation of parliament. Even the question of constitutionality has been dragged in as an argument to oppose this idea. It has been said that it would not be in keeping with the supremacy of parliament to deal with wage rates, wage increases, working conditions and other benefits relating to civil servants and that in effect that is what a bill such as this would do. It has been said that parliament would be giving to an outside body, a conciliation board, the right to determine and decide what salary rates would be.
From time to time over the years parliament has undertaken to relieve itself of some of its functions and obligations, some of its authority and power. I will mention only a few examples of situations where parliament thought it wise to divest itself of its tight control and authority over certain matters. For instance, the Expropriation Act passed by the Canadian parliament provides that a body outside parliament will have the right to decide what price will be paid for land expropriated by the crown if there is a difference of opinion as to what the actual value of the land is. In this instance parliament divested itself of that authority and control.
The Civil Service Act itself and the establishment of the civil service commission are another example where parliament has divested itself of certain authority and control over the employment of people in the public service. Neither parliament nor the government has any authority or control, and I do not think they should have, over the establishment of qualifications, hiring procedures or employment practices with respect to people entering the civil service. The Crown Liability Act is another statute under which the crown has given up certain rights, power and authority that it had at one time. Crown corporations, -all of which were established by acts of parliament, are covered by the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. In fact, at the present time one crown corporation is engaged in negotiations with the unions in that particular field, and I refer to the railway industry. The provisions of the act apply there.
I think the time is long past when parliament and the government should have divested themselves of their tight control over the wages paid to civil servants and not have continued what is in effect rank discrimination against a group of employees in this nation. To continue the law as it stands now and in effect to treat civil servants as if they were second class citizens 79951-0-51
Industrial Relations Act because they happen to work for the government makes somewhat of a mockery of the bill of rights which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has been talking about for so long. If there are rights and principles to be established so that justice will be equitably applied, these rights and principles should apply across the board to all employees whether they work for the Department of Labour under the direction of the Minister of Labour or whether they work for Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines or any of the other crown corporations. I do not know of any reason in the world why the 120,000 or more employees of a particular employer, the government of Canada, should be treated with the scorn and disdain with which they have been treated for many years and which is getting worse.
There is no reason why the government should persist in denying to its employees the same rights it has guaranteed to employees of private employers and employees of crown corporations. During election campaigns practically all the cabinet ministers like to gloat over these hollow cliches about fairness and equality and yet refuse to put these same principles of equality, fairness and justice into effect for employees working for the government.
For a number of years I was an officer of a union which was certified under British Columbia law and dealt with employers in industry. During that period of time we ran into a number of employers whose attitude and feelings in the labour-management field were excellent. They treated their employees with complete justice, complete fairness and complete equity. The employers would approach the bargaining table with an uncomplicated desire to reach collective agreement and to see that the best possible conditions and wages, and so on, were forthcoming to employees working for them.
During the course of the activities in that same field we ran into employers who were cheap and chiselling in their activities toward the employees. This government in its dealings with its employees, is just about as cheap and chiselling as any private industry I have run into, if one can judge by what has happened to the civil service recently. If the attitude that this government showed toward its employees in the public service had occurred in private industry by a private employer it would have had a strike the next morning without any question at all. The government should be thankful that it has not forced its own employees into that sort of action. It should be thankful for the loyalty that exists among the civil servants,

Industrial Relations Act a loyalty to the crown and to the operation of government services. But it is a bit of administrative immorality to exploit that loyalty for political or other reasons, and that is precisely what this government has been doing and what they intend to continue to do, apparently.
We have heard quite a bit of discussion recently about the possibility of an election next year. One of the reasons why we may expect to have an election next year is that the Prime Minister does not want to injure himself in his own province by participating in, or being accused of participating in, a scheme that will reduce the representation from Saskatchewan. But if there is an election next year it will be seen that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and his colleagues in the government have changed their attitude in their dealings with the civil service and that a wage increase will be forthcoming. It will probably be coincidental and come at the same time as an election, but there is ample precedent for it. This government likes to fall back on precedents established over the last 22 years.
Whenever we raise some question as to the propriety of government taking certain action they drag out the dusty old Hansards when the Liberals were in office and say, "This is what they did, and this is what we should do, also." I am sure they are going to follow precisely the same line in so far as the civil servant's salaries are concerned and use them as a political gimmick and hope to buy some sort of favour at election time. But this is apart from the thoughts contained in the bill itself.
I am very much afraid that with the growing insistence from employees in the public service, the growing insistence for equity, fairness, justice and good treatment, if this government does not agree with the need to apply equitably our laws to all people, whether they work in the civil service or not, this parliament and government will be participating in the destruction of that loyalty which does exist in the public service of Canada. It would be extremely unfortunate if we were to do that sort of thing.
The bill refers to certain, specific things, but apparently it does not meet with the complete approval of everyone in the civil service. Of course, it would be a strange state of affairs if it did, if 120,000 people were to say, "Yes, we agree explicitly with the ideas contained in the bill," but I think it is generally supported. However, there is one place, or there is one prominent individual in the civil service in British Columbia with whom this sort of proposal does not find favour. I do not like at any time to use my


privileged position in this bouse to make reference to or comments on someone outside the house. Perhaps I can say in this instance, as should be stated in all instances, that where it is necessary-and I intend to do this-to mention the name of an individual who is not in the house and has not the same protection that members of the house have, I am quite prepared to make the same comments outside the house, if that is the desire of the individual to whom I intend to make reference.
In this regard I will read from an article in "DVA Crew's Aider", a mimeographed publication of the Department of Veterans Affairs employees, dated January, 1960. On page 2 of this issue there is a reference by a gentleman in British Columbia about myself and about this particular bill. If the house will grant me the indulgence of a minute or two I shall read a paragraph and make reference to it. I read:
Stan Stonier, chairman of the joint action committee for B.C., said that Mr. Frank Howard, C.C.F., M.P. for Skeena, has presented a bill to repeal section 55 of the labour act and thus permit civil servants to engage in collective bargaining. "I am afraid this action will do more harm than good," said Mr. Stonier, "as the government does not take kindly to legislation proposed by members of other parties."
Mr. Stonier must be under the impression that we in fact do have a one-party state. I disagree with him in this respect. I am sure everyone will disagree with the implication in that regard. I continue with the quotation:
In my opinion Mr. Howard's action may delay collective bargaining as much as five years.
I think Mr. Stonier is doing more damage to the desires and hopes of his own organization than he realizes when he makes statements and comments such as these. We all know that in some instances this government does look kindly on legislation proposed by private members. We do not, of course, think that they look as kindly as they should on everything we propose, but in some instances this government has followed the lead suggested by private members in this house. Private members in the opposition have sometimes introduced legislation that has later become law. I can do no better than point to legislation that I proposed since I came here, namely the granting of the right to vote in federal elections to our native Indian population. We find that this government has introduced some bills along that line this year and they will be debated sometime during this session. I think Mr. Stonier should have a better understanding of this kind of thing and of the way this government operates. I do not know what his political persuasion is. If he is under the erroneous impression that

the government does not take kindly to legislation proposed by members of other parties, then he should pay a bit more attention to the manner in which parliament functions and the fact that private members and opposition members have won support for certain things over the years.
I am sure that the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) would not agree, even in their wildest moments, that because a proposal is made by an opposition party, or by an opposition member, it will thereby be delayed for another four or five years, as Mr. Stonier suggested. In fact I think the duty falls upon the Minister of Labour, whose responsibility it is to administer the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, to write a letter to Mr. Stonier and straighten him out on his misunderstanding. I know the Minister of Labour is a very kind and genial man and likes to have everything in its proper place and to see fairness applied. I am sure he would not wish to have Mr. Stonier labouring under the misunderstanding that this government does not take kindly to legislation proposed by members of other parties. Incidentally, I would greatly appreciate it if the minister, when he writes this letter, would send me a copy of it so that I may put it in my files for future reference in case the question is raised again by Mr. Stonier.
We hear all sorts of references, Mr. Speaker, to activities in other nations, about how we decry them when we hear that forms of discrimination are taking place in other nations. We look very unkindly-although we may not say so officially as a nation-at the apartheid action in South Africa. Certainly society in Canada looks unkindly on it. We look with extreme distaste upon the discrimination that took place in Little Rock, Arkansas a little while ago in connection with education. We should look with equal distaste and scorn upon our own activities in discriminating against the civil servants of this nation by continuing to bind them to a sort of cap-in-hand attitude any time they want an adjustment in their salary structures. We should not at least be proud of the fact that this parliament, by its inaction over the years, has placed the civil servants in the position of being almost beggars, coming and pleading with their employer for an adjustment in their salary structure, even though those adjustments may be recommended by the civil service commission and even though the Minister of Finance may hide the documents because they are embarrassing to him in that they contain references to certain suggested wage increases which I understand are in the neighbourhood of a 10 per cent across the board adjustment.

We should not be proud of the fact that we do things of this sort, that we treat 120,000 of our employees in such a distasteful manner, thinking that the civil servants-and this is what we are doing-should live in a period of 150 years ago when the relationship between an employee and an employer was one of master and servant, with the servant having no rights at all. We have advanced a bit beyond that stage, apparently because the civil service employees have some rights. One of them is to say, "Please may we have an adjustment in our wages". Another one is to take their caps off and say, "I hope, Mr. Employer, that you will be kind enough to do this". We say they have that sort of right but we will not go all the way and make this principle of collective bargaining rights universally applicable to employees of the federal government as well as to employees all across Canada who come under the jurisdiction of this particular parliament.
I do not intend to say too much more, Mr. Speaker, except that I am quite sure that there is no possibility, at least on this particular day, of our engaging in a vote on this particular bill although I should certainly like to see one. If I may expand on that thought a bit, I should like to say again, as I have said on other occasions, that bills of this type, bills that are in the hands of a private member, are the ones that parliament and the government should consider above everything else by allowing them to come to an individual free vote, even though we may be obliged to sit a few extra days in the session in order to achieve that purpose. Ideas of this sort proposed by private members, whether they come from one side of the house or the other, should all be allowed to come to a free vote in order to determine the wishes of parliament in a free and democratic manner and what it desires to do on a particular idea propounded by a particular private member.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion during the session on which I have had an opportunity to rise in my place and to extend to you publicly my congratulations on your being appointed Deputy Speaker, to congratulate the mover (Mr. Morissette) and the seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne and to congratulate the newly appointed Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) and the various parliamentary secretaries who now have taken on higher responsibilities.
We are dealing here with an area of humanity for whom we have the highest regard. They are people who have displayed over the years a distinction in the service
804	HOUSE OF
Industrial Relations Act of their country which is unequalled anywhere in the world and whom we all as members of the House of Commons hold in the highest respect and regard. Hence when I hear the sponsor, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), using the language he used in trying to establish his point of view with regard to our dealings as a government with the public service in Canada, I can hardly countenance any support for a bill proposed in the manner in which he proposed it.
It was early in December, I think, that we members in the city of Winnipeg had the opportunity of going into this matter with the civil servants in the greater Winnipeg area and from other parts of the province of Manitoba. At the outset I can say that they ran probably one of the most efficient meetings held anywhere under the auspices of the joint action committee of the civil servants throughout the entire country. Their attitude and their courtesy and the hearing we received were typical of the general stability in the general labour market of the greater Winnipeg area, something for which we have been noted for many years.
Like other hon. members, on that occasion we did not have before us the recommendations of the pay research bureau nor did we know what were the contents of the properly confidential report of the civil service commission. We were obliged to hear out the arguments of the able representatives of the service in that area and to speak to them without any factual knowledge of just exactly how they stood up having regard to a comparison with the wages paid to employees in the civil and provincial services, for example, in the area and paid by general employers of labour in the industry and commerce of our city. As I pointed out, they carried on the meeting with respect and distinction not notable elsewhere in Canada, and generally speaking we were well satisfied with the hearing.
We should remember, of course, that the employees of the civil service are not our employees, as was implied in the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena, but are the employees of the citizens of Canada; that the citizens of Canada are the people who direct us in what they feel their requirements are; and that we, in simple words, are their servants. Hence, when we deal with their requests, as they have been ably dealt with by the executive council, I am sure we must bear in mind the general concensus of our masters, the people of Canada.
During the early hearings of this important issue on the merits as to whether or not our service was entitled to a raise, the general
[Mr. Chown.l

concensus of opinion of the people in my constituency was that the decision of our cabinet was correct. These are the people whom I serve, and all my hon. colleagues do likewise. This was the task they reposed on us, and whether the case for an increase in pay on the part of civil servants has merit or not, we must act in accordance with their instructions.
However, I did say at the meeting in Winnipeg that I favoured the principle of collective bargaining. I said this because for some three years I negotiated the contract with the civic employees of Winnipeg on behalf of the citizens of Winnipeg. In those negotiations we always felt that we arrived at a scale of pay in all classifications commensurate with the service rendered by the man concerned, as compared with the general rate of pay for the same classification for like employees in the greater Winnipeg area, and indeed in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, which we used as our yardstick as well. With one exception, I think the relations between the corporation of the city of Winnipeg and its employees have been extremely smooth, because our side brings a sense of responsibility to the bargaining table which represents the point of view on labour's side, as much of the taxpayers, as it does on the side of the members of the city council who were carrying on the negotiations.
What comes to mind when I read the contents of this bill is the fact that it seems to be in conflict with the Civil Service Act itself. It is not untypical of the C.C.F. to be striking at the supremacy of parliament and suggesting that we shed ourselves of our responsibility to the people of Canada by simply throwing out to some independent agency the responsibility of spending millions and millions of dollars, giving them carte blanche to go ahead and do as they please with the people who are serving the citizens of Canada. One does not have to think too hard about what the reaction across the nation would be if we did so shed ourselves of this tremendous responsibility.
With regard to the point of conflict at law to which I referred, if you read the Civil Service Act, being chapter 48, volume 2, of the revised statutes of Canada, 1952, subsection 11(1) reads:
The commission shall, from time to time, as may be necessary, recommend rates of compensation for any new classes that may be established hereunder, and may propose changes in the rates of compensation for existing classes.
Subsection (2) provides, in short, that there shall be a minimum and a maximum in each classification, and that the responsibility for any increments given as authorized on four occasions during the year would

be the responsibility of the deputy minister. Then subsection (3) reads:
Proposed rates of compensation shall become operative only upon their approval by the governor in council, and, where any increased expenditure will result therefrom, when parliament has provided the money required for such increased expenditure.
So it comes back to us, likewise servants of the citizens of Canada, and quite rightly so, to make the ultimate decision about any changes in classification or pay rates which may occur in our service. I think this is a conflict of law which would make the bill proposed by the hon. member for Skeena ultra vires of this parliament. Certainly, as I see it, we would be called to task by the people of Canada if we ever allowed such a bill to pass.
One of the things that we should remember, out of respect for the loyalty of our public servants, is that you can be sure that the minister responsible, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), has given every opportunity for a hearing on any occasion on which it was sought, that he has been courteous, understanding, sympathetic, and has done all in his power to reconcile the needs of the civil service paywise with the responsibility he has for the fiscal and monetary policies of our government. This is not to suggest that the contents of the confidential report of the civil service commission necessarily recommended an increase, or perhaps recommended increases, in certain classifications. But it does suggest to me, knowing the hon. minister as I do, as well as his colleagues, that the door was always open until the final conclusion was reached, and even today remains open to the agents of the civil service on any occasion they wish to see him to bring up any particular grievance they have in connection with pay rates.
However, notwithstanding the decision of the executive council made a short time ago, increases have been allowed, as indicated in the statement of the minister, where he said that in certain cases where a classification was suffering in comparison with a similar classification in other areas of employment an increase would be granted. This was the case with the nursing sisters, and the amount of the increase was sufficient to bring the federal government back into the recruiting field for that particular classification, which was undoubtedly the objective, and the reason why they were not able to retain their nursing staffs. This to me indicated that they were having with other classifications no difficulty in recruiting.
Before I went to the meeting in the civic auditorium of the city of Winnipeg, I learned from the local commissioner that, by and
Industrial Relations Act large, there was no problem in recruiting. Then apart from the other features of our service, the fringe benefits, the recent addition of medical health insurance, and the fact that even at their present rates of pay, in certain regions of our country that rate of pay, being equalized as it is across the nation, is deemed probably by civil servants to be adequate. I think that civil servants who are employed in Newfoundland and the maritimes would feel that they were being reasonably well cared for. In other areas, heavy industrial areas, there is probably some hardship. But we have confidence that the government in course of time will meet any real grievance, and meet it adequately.
Just for a moment I should like to dwell on the entire problem of giving to the civil service bargaining rights. As I said before, I subscribe to this in principle; it is just a matter of how it is to be executed without this conflict of law to which I referred. Ultimately, if there is going to be what the hon. member improperly called a conciliation board-it should be called an arbitration board-if there is going to be arbitration, that arbitration must be by the executive council. That is one vital point with regard to which I must disagree with the hon. member because of the explanation which I gave earlier. I do not think it is unreasonable that a committee of cabinet could act as arbitrators if the civil service were given bargaining rights, but I believe this is something which would have to be done by way of amendment to the Civil Service Act, perhaps in conjunction with an amendment to the industrial disputes investigation act. This is something which should be looked into with the greatest of care and it could perhaps be tied in with the terms of reference to be given to the Hoover style of commission which is to be set up in accordance with the announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
For the moment I think this bill is one which, on legal grounds, none of us could support. Moreover, none of us could fail to recognize that it goes to the core of the sovereignty of the parliament in which we sit, and none of us could fail to feel some disappointment with the manner of the presentation of the bill by the hon. member concerned, couched as it was in the language he used. I think if he expects to gain support, as I would expect to gain support from him, he must on no occasion run down the dignity and responsibility of the executive council and speak of it as cheap and chiselling or politically immoral, or speak of it as treating our public servants with scorn and disdain-words from the back alleys which

Industrial Relations Act have no application when we are speaking of the type of people who are involved in a bill of this nature.
I will close my remarks by saying I support the principle of collective bargaining in this connection and feel that after intelligent examination a bill or bills could be brought in which would preserve the rights of parliament yet give to the civil service the right to bargain at a round table which they have been seeking for so many years.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a few words, and a few words only, because I do not want to be accused of killing this bill by speaking until six o'clock. Right at the start, I want to point out to the house, as did the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown), that the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) were not always accurate, particularly when he maintained that, for the past 22 years, federal civil servants had been treated in a distasteful manner. This is an inaccuracy he should not have committed.
I even recall that, during the period from 1930 to 1935, it was necessary, because of certain circumstances, to reduce the salaries of federal civil servants by 10 per cent, but it cannot be said that they were ill-treated, for living costs had gone down to such an extent that, even after the reduction, federal government employees enjoyed a very privileged position compared with that of other workers.
Besides, civil servants have had at least six salary increases since the end of the war. It is only in the last two years, or just about, that this difficulty has cropped up. I don't want to accuse anyone, but the trouble is there just the same. As a result of the increase in the cost of living, civil servants have asked for salary increases, and submitted requests to the government to that effect.
Last year, following the recommendation of the civil service commission, which did not approve the desired increase, their request was turned down. This year again, their request was turned down, in spite of a secret report which probably does approve the increases requested by civil servants.
We are dealing with human beings who have certain rights, even though they are government employees. Civil servants have a right to state their case, because it is an

inalienable right, a natural right that we
have and one that overrides all other rights that may be granted by man. A man has a right to defend his way of life. The working conditions and salaries of federal civil servants must be settled, if possible, on a friendly basis, but in any event they must be settled in some way by the employer.
As I have indicated in another debate, there are civil servants who are in straitened circumstances.
A few days ago, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) answered one of my questions, and we now know that 37,439 civil servants earn less than $3,000, and that 53,840 civil servants earn less than $4,000 a year.
This means that a considerable number of civil servants are forced to hold the line, while employees of private enterprise across the country are able to get increases to match the cost of living.
For that reason, can we fully accept the proposition of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard)? I am not sure, but I know that something must be done. It must be recognized that civil servants have a right to be heard so that they might know just why the government chaoses to grant or deny their request.
I realize that they have enjoyed statutory increases fairly regularly. But can we settle that question on our own without first consulting civil servants? We submit that they should be heard by the government.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I submit that if parliament wants to go into the problem of civil employees we should at least give them a chance to make their representations.
For my part, regardless of whether we are in favour or not of granting civil servants bargaining rights, I believe the matter should be submitted to the industrial relations committee. The committee could consider requests made by federal civil servants' organizations. Those organizations could clarify the situation and tell us whether they really want bargaining rights.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg South pointed out, it is perhaps a constitutional matter, one that we cannot settle. I know that in England civil servants have bargaining and arbitration rights and that the arbitration committee submits a report to parlia-

ment, which, ultimately, takes a decision. That is the practice over there, because parliament must be, after all, the supreme authority to decide on matters involving public expenditures.
Mr. Speaker, there might be another way of reaching the same objective, though it is not provided in the bill before us. I am convinced that if the civil service organizations were allowed two representatives within the civil service commission, to deal with questions of salaries or working conditions, federal employees would be able to state their case. Thus, in similar circumstances, there would no longer be any allegedly secret report, which the government does not want to disclose to the Canadian public. I think this might be the best way to settle the question, because the final decision would be parliament's.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to labour the point but I know that in certain quarters it is claimed that civil servants are well paid. However, they have not been granted an increase since 1957, though the living cost index, which was then 121.6, had risen to 127.9 in December 1959.
This means there is a gap between the income level of those employees and the cost of living, or what they have to spend to support their families. And if the government is unable to settle the matter as was the practice in the past, something has to be done. We should either pass this bill, or refer it to the industrial relations committee where representatives of civil servant organizations may state their case.
However, I insist that something be done, and as soon as possible, because civil servants cannot put up indefinitely with the conditions being forced upon them by government.

Mr. Speaker, as I have only a couple of minutes at my disposal I shall have to confine myself to one or two extremely important points. There is one point that has not as yet been raised in this debate. I was surprised and somewhat shocked to see a bill of this type in the form in which it is drafted brought in by a supporter of the C.C.F. party. The bill proposes to make certain amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. It may be an oversight but it is certainly surprising to me that the sponsor of the bill neglected to make any reference to section 28. If we were to pass this bill it would mean that disputes between the federal government and the civil service of Canada would be determined finally and without any further recourse by a three-man conciliation board.
Industrial Relations Act
The act provides-and there has been no effort made to amend it-that each party to the dispute, which in this case would be the government and the civil service association, must appoint one man each to the three-man board, the third member being nominated by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). Consequently we have a bill sponsored by a member of the C.C.F. group requesting this government to make it law that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will appoint one member of the board, the civil service association will appoint a second member and the Minister of Labour will appoint the third and final member. Surely that is not what we would want to see in this country. That section would have to be amended before I could support the bill.
Another point which I consider of some significance is that the civil service commission in its annual report makes reference to the fact that in normal times adjustments in salary should be on a class by class basis rather than general across the board increases. That statement in the report is qualified when we have inflation or outstanding increases in the industrial wage of the country, but in normal times the commission has recommended class by class increases.
We have in Canada at the present time approximately 1,900 classes of employees in the federal service. The act in question which is to be amended makes it mandatory for this three-man board, constituted as I suggested, to bring in a report to the Minister of Labour within a period of 14 days after its appointment. I can see a conciliation board in 14 days, and during a longer period of time if agreed to by the parties, bringing in a report dealing with employees in the automobile industry, or a report concerning coal miners or steel workers where most of the people concerned have uniform skills and an equal right, but with 1,900 various classifications it would be impossible for a three-man board appointed on the spur of the moment to do justice to such a problem.
As it is nearly six o'clock I shall make just one more point before resuming my seat. I am definitely in favour of some form of collective bargaining for the civil servants of this country. I am not, however, in favour of the approach adopted today in the hon. member's bill. I feel quite confident that we are near the period in the history of this country when our civil servants will achieve something in the nature of collective bargaining. It is now appreciated by management and accepted by labour not only in the great industries of Canada but also in the crown corporations for which the government is responsible.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.
